core_claim: The story of 17,525 NTSB-investigated U.S. small-plane accidents over 2010-2024 is the gap between what is common and what is lethal — engine failures show up in nearly a quarter of investigations but kill 13% of the people involved, while spatial disorientation appears in fewer than 2% and kills 95%.
tension: Most pilots are trained to fear an engine quitting at low altitude. Most news coverage focuses on the spectacular multi-fatality crashes. Neither is what the data says you should worry most about.
payoff: After reading, a non-pilot understands the actual geometry of small-plane risk in the United States — and that three conditions (instrument weather, night, maneuvering) explain more than half of every death in the dataset.
title: What Kills Small-Plane Pilots
subtitle: Fifteen years of NTSB findings, 2010-2024

edt_01.label: Hook — the 95% number
edt_01.title: The 95% number
edt_01.editorial_notes: 95.0% spatial disorientation fatal share must stay exact. Engine failure 12.7% must stay exact. The contrast between the two numbers is the lead.

edt_02.label: What you're looking at
edt_02.title: What you're looking at
edt_02.editorial_notes: Use this section to anchor the reader: 17,525 events, fifteen years, FAR Part 91. The 98.5% probable-cause-text coverage is the unique feature that makes the rest of the piece possible — flag it.

edt_03.label: The fifteen-year trend
edt_03.title: Fifteen years
edt_03.editorial_notes: Pair the FAA per-100k-hour benchmark from det_03 with our dataset's accident-count trend. The seasonality inversion (counts peak summer, fatal share peaks winter) is a worth-mentioning curiosity but not the main chart of this section.

edt_04.label: Common vs. lethal — the centerpiece
edt_04.title: Common is not lethal
edt_04.editorial_notes: THIS is the centerpiece chart of the whole piece. Designer should encode every cause-pattern as a point on a chart with x = events_count (or log scale) and y = fatal_share_pct. Quadrant labels: rare-and-lethal (upper-left), common-and-lethal (upper-right), common-and-survivable (lower-right). Spatial disorientation should be visually highlighted as the upper-left extremum. The chart MUST include axes labeled with both dimensions clearly.

edt_05.label: VFR into IMC
edt_05.title: Into the clouds
edt_05.editorial_notes: The chart should make the weather × flight-plan-class structure visible — IMC-NONE at 74.5% fatal needs to read as the dataset's most-extreme survivable-looking decision. Mention the 178-seconds factoid from det_05 in prose.

edt_06.label: After dark
edt_06.title: After dark
edt_06.editorial_notes: Dark-night (NDRK) at 55.6% fatal is the bar to highlight. Designer can use a single horizontal bar chart with the lighting subcategories sorted by fatal share.

edt_07.label: Geography & Alaska paradox
edt_07.title: The Alaska paradox
edt_07.editorial_notes: A U.S. state-level choropleth (events count) with Alaska highlighted is the obvious primary visual. Pair with a small inset showing AK vs rest-of-US fatal share difference (9.6% vs 18.2%) so the paradox doesn't get buried in the choropleth's color scale.

edt_08.label: The fleet that won't quit
edt_08.title: Old planes, old patterns
edt_08.editorial_notes: The 39-year median fleet age is the surprising statistic for general readers. Designer should make this the visual hook. The homebuilt 1.28× vs det_04's 4× distinction MUST be in the prose — it is a common misconception correction. Cessna/Piper/Beech share-of-accidents can be a sidebar stat callout.

edt_09.label: What it adds up to
edt_09.title: What it adds up to
edt_09.editorial_notes: The Lockhart balloon NTSB quote MUST appear verbatim. End on the 'upper-left is still there' line. No summary, no call-to-action. Designer should consider an atmospheric image of clouds, dusk, or open sky — something that evokes the conditions discussed without showing a wreck.
